newsitem.title: UK: Euro products outlook - gas oil bounce seen.
newsitem.headline: Euro products outlook - gas oil bounce seen.

text.p: European gas oil and fuel oil were bullish on restricted supply, low stocks and strong demand, but gasoline could slip relative to crude this week, traders said.

Last week's dramatic fall in gas oil prices was a temporary setback in a major bull run which would resume shortly, they added, predicting further increases in the premium for Europe's new low sulphur diesel.
"I expect gas oil to recover very strongly next week," said a products trading manager at a major oil company. "In fact nothing has changed in the physical market."
"If anything it is even tighter because stocks are getting lower and lower," he said.
European distillate stocks fell by three million barrels in September, ending the month 4.5 million tonnes below last year, according to the latest data from Euroilstock.
The trading manager expected the Brent/gas oil crack spread, which fell by $1.50 last week to $6.50 per barrel on Friday, to return to $8 this week.
"I see the crack spread around $8, not above it, because an $8 crack is in line with a $3 refining margin," he said.
The differential between 0.05 and 0.2 percent sulphur gas oil, now at $20 per tonne, was expected to hit $30 by the end of the month.
"The UK, France and Germany are incredibly tight on diesel. There are no stocks at all, so even a minor problem in a refinery is a nightmare," said one.

A cracked pipeline at Shell's Pernis refinery earlier this month forced the company into a huge buying spree on the barge markets. One refiner said: "What happened is that refiners invested just the minimum and did not invest to produce more than core business.
"In the past, when you ran sweet crude, you could get 0.2 percent sulphur gas oil without using any other units like hydrotreaters, desulphurisers and reformers," he added.
"Now, to make 0.05 you need sweet crude and all these units running. If there is one failure in the system you are unable to produce 0.05 percent."
"The differential could go to the roof. I would not be surprised to see $30 by the end of October."
Low stocks was also a factor behind traders' bullish predictions on the high sulphur fuel oil market.
Increasing winter demand, especially in Romania, falling Russian exports and fuel oil's cheapness relative to crude were other factors.
Sweet crud runs also meant less fuel being produced. Traders expected high sulphur to rise by $2.00-4.00 per tonne.
Gasoline was expected to come under pressure. With desulphurisation units requiring large volumes of hydrogen, refiners are expected to run their platformers at full capacity.
"I think we might see gasoline underperforming against crude," said one trader.
